newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian economy said slowed by political quarrels.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian economy said slowed by political quarrels.

text.p: Bosnia's economy has slowed this summer after a rapid revival, partly because political quarrels in the peacetime government delayed pledges of fresh reconstruction aid, foreign analysts said on Monday.

"There are all kinds of indications that the rate of economic growth from last year and the first half of this year is coming to an end," an analyst with the office of the international High Representative to Bosnia told Reuters.
Industrial output fell 10.6 percent in July in the Moslem-Croat federation, which covers half the country, and industrial prices rose only 0.2 percent, according to state statistics.
"Unchanged industrial prices fit in with reports that industrial production was depressed," the analyst said.
More than $1 billion in reconstruction aid donated to Bosnia in 1996 has helped fuel a strong peacetime recovery in the Moslem-Croat federation
The federation economy enjoyed a 50 percent growth rate last year and the World Bank has estimated that the economy will grow at about 30 to 35 percent this year.

But private investors, both domestic and foreign, were discouraged by the postponement of an international fund-raising conference for Bosnia which was held in July after months of delays, analysts said.
Donors pledged about $1.2 billion in postwar aid, less than the goal of $1.4 billion set by organisers.
"Speculation that there would be no money from a donors' conference must have had a negative effect on expectations of investors," another foreign expert said.
"In addition, demand for industrial products, which to a large extent are building materials, fell because new projects were not feasible this year without donors' money."

The donors' conference was postponed because Bosnian political leaders in the central multi-ethnic government failed to agree on basic economic legislation, including a law on a central bank and common currency.
By the time rival leaders approved the legislative package in June, much of the building season had passed.
Some foreign experts said the reported 10.6 percent decrease in industrial output might reflect a change in how the government calculates economic statistics.
"I suspect this might be a correction of statistics data, because these figures indicate a break in the trend which we don't see in reality," another analyst, who asked not to be named, said.
The state statistics agency in its August report said output declined because electric power production fell due to low water levels and decreased demand by consumers in the summer months.

"Industrial production should not have shifted so much on a month-to-month basis only due to electric energy. The overall decline had to be much less than quoted in the agency's report," the analyst said.
Bosnia's other entity, the Serb republic, has experienced only marginal growth.

The Serb entity has received only about two percent of all reconstruction aid because nationalist Bosnian Serb leaders have refused to meet donor requirements to abide by the terms of a peace treaty. --Sarajevo newsroom ,+387-71-663-864
